newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mourning Algeria pay last respects to slain unionist.
newsitem.headline: Mourning Algeria pay last respects to slain unionist.

text.p: Algerians flowed into trade union headquarters on Thursday to pay their last respects to assassinated union leader Abdelhak Benhamouda before his burial in a cemetery reserved for Algeria's martyrs.
Hundreds of mourners headed in a steady flow through the building in the capital Algiers where Benhamouda's body was on display.
"Police have blocked off some of the roads leading to the building, and stopped cars going through," one witness said.
The security was a sombre reminder of bomb attacks in the capital and other cities which, like Benhamouda's killing, have been blamed by the authorities on Moslem fundamentalists.
Otherwise, discreet security was in place around the central May 1st Square where Benhamouda, a staunch supporter of President Liamine Zeroual, was gunned down on Tuesday.
Algerian residents and state-run radio said traffic stopped across Algeria at 1 p.m. (1200 GMT) in response to a call by Benhamouda's union to observe one minute of silence for his memory.
Inside the imposing union building, Benhamouda's body lay in a coffin covered with the national green and white flag, and surrounded by wreaths.
Six men from the civil protection service surrounded the coffin, at one end of which stood a portrait of the dead man.
Verses being intoned from the Moslem holy book, the Koran, was the only sound inside the room where the body lay, apart from occasional outbursts of grief from mourners.
"One elderly woman collapsed in tears as she passed the coffin, while another shouted out 'We will not give way to terrorism'," said Algeria's official news agency APS.
Despite the government blaming Moslem rebels, independent newspapers and many ordinary Algerians asked whether they, or political rivals, were behind the killing.
Benhamouda's last words -- "Kamel, my brother, they have betrayed us" -- gasped out before he died and reported by an Algerian newspaper, added to the mystery.

Among those paying their respects, APS said, were government ministers and foreign envoys. Algerian state radio said unionists from the United States, Nicole Notat from the French CFDT main union, representing European movements, and others from neighbouring Tunisia and Morocco, also attended.
"It is the same as the day when we mourned (president Mohamed) Boudiaf," a woman trade unionist said, recalling his June 1992 assassination after six months in power.
Another woman said: "We lost the father of the poor and the defender of workers' rights."
"If the killers aimed to destroy the union through slaying Benhamouda, they are very much mistaken," said another mourner.
Tributes poured in from Algerian organisations and from abroad for the man known as one of Zeroual's strongest political allies.
His million-strong Union Generale des Travailleurs Algerience (UGTA) said on Wednesday that Benhamouda would be buried in in El-Alia cemetery later on Thursday.
The cemetery in the Algerian capital is reserved for leaders from the 1954-1962 war of independence against France and for those regarded as having died a martyr's death since.
Benhamouda's final words, the ambush in central Algiers and the escape in the heavily-policed city of the four gunmen raised a clamour of questions over his killing and its motives.
Algeria's independent newspapers all asked: "Who killed Benhamouda?", a powerful figure only in his 40s who was preparing to start his own political party.
Liberte asked whether he died because he was "the new political man who was preparing...to upset the national chessboard...Who killed him, or rather, who ordered his elimination?"
The government-controlled El Moudjahid said: "It is not easy to understand this killing and the reasons which truly motivated it."
The UGTA called for a total work stoppage except for emergency services for Saturday, the first working day of the Algerian week.
Benhamouda, a vociferous anti-Islamist, recently expressed disillusion with Algeria's political hierarchy, saying it had done nothing to resolve five years of crisis.
About 60,000 people have been killed in the conflict which erupted in 1992 after the authorities cancelled a general election dominated by Islamists. New elections are promised before July this year.
